title: Round 10 - Gate S' applied, and the desk drops its best performer
focus: Apply the repaired stability gate, Gate S', which replaces round 9's level bar with a coverage clause and a pure dispersion clause and makes the seat count an output rather than a fixed target, to the same body of evidence round 9 already used.
headline: The repaired rule seated only B-momentum and C-trend, dropping A-rotation - the desk's best live performer at over 65% since inception - purely on backtest rank dispersion, and the desk owner then overrode that and kept A-rotation on the desk anyway, citing its live record.
outcome:
Round 10 recomputes the same body of evidence round 9 used rather than re-running anything, since re-running a frozen tournament over an unchanged store would read as independent confirmation of a single measurement. Gate A and Gate L reproduced round 9's results unchanged.

Gate S' has two clauses and no level term: a result must appear on at least two of three historical matrices, never imputed, and the dispersion across whatever matrices the card actually ran must not exceed a range of three ranks. Four cards cleared it - B-momentum, B4-tight-stop, C-trend and H-trend-diversified - all with a rank range of one or two. B3-concentrated, the card round 8's rule had preferred before being overridden, failed at a range of four, meaning the repaired gate now excludes it without needing an override. A-rotation failed for a substantive reason this time: it ranked 10th of fifteen on one bear-weighted matrix and 1st on the ladder, the largest rank swing in the field.

Distinctness then seated B-momentum over its own family and C-trend over H-trend-diversified in a trend-seat contest decided by only 0.22 points, flagged as unsettled rather than a settled ranking.

The result was two ranked seats of a possible four, for the second round running, but framed as an expected output of a no-floor rule rather than a shortfall needing escalation. What it cost was real: the desk's best live performer, A-rotation at over 65% since inception and roughly 37% out-of-sample, was replaced by C-trend, which was slightly negative live.

The desk owner then overrode the rule's output and kept A-rotation on the desk, on the side of the live record rather than the backtest dispersion measure. The document frames this as the second override in three rounds, both going the same direction: rounds 8 and 10 each ranked purely on backtests, and the owner weighted live evidence the rule is structurally unable to see, because no gate scores whether a card is right, only whether it is alive.
owner_override: Gate S' dropped A-rotation, the desk's best live performer (over +65% since inception, roughly +37% out-of-sample), in favor of C-trend, on the grounds that A-rotation's backtest rank swings from 10th of fifteen on one historical matrix to 1st on another - the largest dispersion in the field. The desk owner overrode this and kept A-rotation on the desk, weighting the live record over the backtest dispersion measure; the rule's own output (B-momentum and C-trend only) is left unchanged and A-rotation is still recorded as failing the gate.
carries_forward: Score the live desk's own matrix and weight it above the backtests - now framed as the only item that matters, recommended in every round since round 6.
The trend seat (C-trend versus H-trend-diversified) is decided by only 0.22 points and should not be treated as settled; the discipline distinctness axis may still be the wrong one for this pairing.

New candidates, not new thresholds, are the binding constraint on widening the desk - the ROTH-MOMENTUM and ROTH-VOLTARGET specifications are the only genuinely new ideas since round 5 and still have no execution path into the tournament.
A-rotation has now been dropped by three different rules in four rounds for three different stated reasons; its status should be watched closely if the live regime turns.
